The earlier MIMO example identifies a 2×2 plant element by element. This one fits the whole
coupled plant jointly: a six-degree-of-freedom suspension running in a closed damping
loop, where every transfer-function element shares the same modal poles. The measurement is
the same Pintelon–Schoukens recipe — one periodic multisine per actuator, a leakage-free
reference FRF, a per-bin noise model — and the new piece is a parametric step on top of it
that ties all the elements to a common set of modes.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## A six-mode demonstration
The twin is a coupled normal-mode plant with six shared modes (representative low-frequency
suspension values), driven through six diagonal velocity dampers. It is a demonstration of
the joint-fit measurement, not a validated suspension model, and six modes are not a proof
that the method scales without limit.
:::

## The plant and the loop

The coupled plant `G(s)` has six shared modal poles; coupling lives in the mode shapes, so
the diagonal elements carry anti-resonance notches and the off-diagonal elements carry
notch-free cross terms. It runs closed: six diagonal velocity dampers act through the input
and output decoupling matrices, so the suspension never sits open while it is measured. The
campaign drives each actuator in turn with a band-limited multisine and reads all drive
monitors and sensors through the live loops.

## Step 1 — the open-loop coupled FRF

Because the twin simulates consistently (`u_drive = S·u_exc`, then `y_sens = G·u_drive`), the
per-bin matrix recovery `G = Y·X⁻¹` returns the open-loop coupled FRF even though the data
were taken closed. That inverse is exact off-resonance but noisy near the resonances, where
the drive monitors are small.

## Step 2 — the rank-1 modal fit

The parametric model shares one set of modal poles `(a_k, b_k)` across all elements and gives
each mode a rank-1 residue `R_k = φ_k ψ_kᵀ` — a sensor mode shape `φ_k` times an actuator mode
shape `ψ_k`. The fit is a sample-ML (IQML) minimization on the raw spectra with a per-bin
weighting, and its Cramér–Rao bound propagates to both a per-bin FRF envelope and a
per-mode `(f0, Q)` uncertainty.

The figure below shows one diagonal element `G[0,0]` and one off-diagonal `G[0,3]`: the
nonparametric `|Gnp|` (markers, noisy near the peaks), the rank-1 `|Gfit|` with its ±1σ band,
and the analytic truth. The parametric fit predicts through the resonances where
the per-bin inverse scatters.

```{python}
#| label: fig-r1-through
#| fig-cap: "Through-resonance recovery on a diagonal element G[0,0] and an off-diagonal element G[0,3]: the rank-1 joint modal fit against the measured FRF and the oracle."
#| code-summary: "Through-resonance recovery — G[0,0] and G[0,3]"
rm.through_resonance_fig()
```

## Modal recovery

All six modal frequencies come back through the loops to ~0.15 %, and the deviations sit
inside the Cramér–Rao bars — the recovered `(fit − truth)` residual and its ±1σ envelope:

```{python}
#| label: fig-r1-modes
#| fig-cap: "Per-mode modal frequency residual (fit − oracle) with the Cramér–Rao σ. Residuals inside the band indicate the bound is the realised one."
#| code-summary: "Modal frequency residual ± CRB, per mode"
rm.modal_recovery_fig()
```

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Recovered modes — truth vs fit ± σ"

```

## The init is data-driven

The fit is started from a peak-pick on the recovered FRF: the summed power
`Σᵢⱼ|Gnp(f)|²` is searched for its six strongest peaks, and those seed the pole frequencies.
No accurate prior is used — the modes are found from the data — which is why the recovery is
the same whether the design model was right or badly wrong.

```{python}
#| label: fig-r1-peakpick
#| fig-cap: "The data-driven initialisation: a peak-pick on the recovered FRF power supplies the starting modal frequencies, so the fit needs no accurate prior."
#| code-summary: "Peak-pick on the recovered FRF power"
rm.peak_pick_fig()
```

## What this shows, and what it does not

On this twin the joint fit recovers all six modal frequencies to ~0.15 % through the live
damping loops, with Q to a few percent and a Cramér–Rao envelope consistent with the
deviations. It is a six-mode demonstration of the rank-1 modal step on a representative
coupled plant — not a validated suspension model, and not a claim that the method scales
without limit. the next test is a higher-order, measured plant under a real decoupling
design.
